Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Generator scaffolding left in: oaicite, [cite: 1], placeholders -- finish the text and read it
- The "it's not X, it's Y" construction -- just state Y
- A bolded word opening a list item as a per-item tag -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- Saying "is" the long way: serves as, boasts, functions as -- use the plain verb
- One-line dramatic fragments: "That's it. That's the whole thing." -- cut them, the preceding sentence already made the point
- Em dashes clustering in one document -- most drafts need 0-2; use commas, periods or parentheses for the rest
- Filler verbs: leverages, facilitates, unlocks -- use a plain verb, or cut the sentence
- A snake_case identifier written as plain prose -- name it in words, or mark it as inline code
- Marketing cliches: "hidden gem", "let's dive in" -- say the specific thing
- The "Not X. Not Y." listing construction -- state the point once
- Stock section skeleton: "Despite its success", "Looking ahead" -- name the specific thing the section is for
- Standalone filler adverbs: undoubtedly, arguably, notably, importantly, ultimately -- most add nothing; cut them unless one is carrying real emphasis
- A banned synonym of one of this project's canonical terms, per its declared lexicon -- one word, one meaning: use the canonical term the word's own note names
- Dramatic turning points with nothing concrete behind them: "Everything changed." -- name the actual event, or cut it

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a short announcement for a new feature in a note-taking app: offline sync. Around 200 words.

Offline sync is now live in version 3.2.

Until now, notes you wrote without a connection sat in a local queue and waited. If you opened the same note on your phone and your laptop before either one reconnected, one version quietly won and the other went away. Several of you wrote to us about losing a paragraph that way.

The new sync engine keeps a full edit history on each device. When you reconnect, it merges the changes character by character instead of picking a winner. Two people typing in different paragraphs of a shared note while both offline will see both paragraphs after they come back online. If you both edit the same sentence, we show you a small comparison and let you choose, rather than deciding for you.

This works on all platforms, though the iOS and Android apps need version 3.2 or later to participate in a merge. Older versions fall back to the old behavior.

You don't need to turn anything on. Sync happens in the background when a connection returns, and notes edited offline now show a small clock icon until they land on the server.

Full technical notes are in our engineering blog post on the merge algorithm.

Offline sync is now live in version 3.2.

Until now, notes you wrote without a connection sat in a local queue and waited. If you opened the same note on your phone and your laptop before either one reconnected, one version quietly won and the other went away. Several of you wrote to us about losing a paragraph that way.

The new sync engine keeps a full edit history on each device. When you reconnect, it merges the changes character by character instead of picking a winner. Two people typing in different paragraphs of a shared note while both offline will see both paragraphs after they come back online. If you both edit the same sentence, we show you a small comparison and let you choose, rather than deciding for you.

The same rules apply when the two devices are both yours. Say you add a heading on your laptop on a plane and rewrite the opening line on your phone in the terminal. Whichever device reconnects first uploads its history, the second one replays its own edits on top, and you end up with the heading and the rewritten line in one note. Order of reconnection changes nothing about the result. If the two devices touched the same words, the note opens with both versions side by side and stays that way until you pick one, so nothing is discarded while you are away from it.

This works on all platforms, though the iOS and Android apps need version 3.2 or later to participate in a merge. Older versions fall back to the old behavior.

You don't need to turn anything on. Sync happens in the background when a connection returns, and notes edited offline now show a small clock icon until they land on the server.

Full technical notes are in our engineering blog post on the merge algorithm.
